title: Question 9
stem:
A Hall probe is placed near to one end of a current-carrying solenoid, as shown in Fig. 9.1.

{{figure:figure_9_1}}

Fig. 9.1

The probe is rotated about the axis $XY$ and is then held in a position so that the Hall voltage is maximum.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: a Hall probe is made from a thin slice of material,
hints: Hint 1: Think about how the Hall voltage is formed - moving charges in the slice are pushed to one face by the magnetic force until the electric force from built-up charge balances it. What would make that balancing voltage larger for the same magnetic field?

Hint 2: Remember that the same probe current is squeezed through the cross-section of the slice. How does making the slice thinner affect the drift speed and the charge separation, and so the measured voltage?
parts.proper_answer: Hall voltage $V_H$ is inversely proportional to thickness $t$, $V_H = BI/ntq$. A thinner slice gives a larger $V_H$ for a given $B$, so greater sensitivity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what creates the Hall voltage**
Imagine current flowing along the slice with magnetic field across it. Each charge $q$ moving at drift speed $v$ feels a magnetic force $F = Bqv$ pushing it sideways. Charges pile up on one face, creating an electric field $E_H$ and voltage $V_H$ across the thickness until $qE_H = Bqv$.

Step 2: **See why thickness matters**
For a slice of thickness $t$, $E_H = V_H/t$, so $V_H/t = Bv$. Also $v = I/(nA q)$ where the cross-sectional area depends on $t$. Combining gives $$V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq}$$ So for fixed $B$, $I$ and material $n$, $V_H$ is proportional to $1/t$. A thin slice gives a much larger, more easily measured voltage.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: in order for consistent measurements of magnetic flux density to be made, the current in the probe must be constant.
hints: Hint 1: The Hall voltage is not caused by the magnetic field alone - it also depends on how many charges per second you push through the slice. If that changed, what would happen to your $V_H$ reading even if $B$ stayed the same?
parts.proper_answer: $V_H$ depends on both $B$ and probe current $I$. $I$ must be constant so that $V_H$ is directly proportional to $B$ only.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link voltage to two inputs**
From $$V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq}$$ you can see $V_H$ grows if either $B$ grows or $I$ grows. To use the probe as a magnetometer you want the scale to read $V_H$ proportional to $B$ alone. That is only true if $I$, $n$, $t$ and $q$ are all fixed, so in practice you keep the probe current constant.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The probe is now rotated through an angle of $360^{\circ}$ about the axis $XY$. At angle $\theta = 0$, the Hall voltage $V_{H}$ has maximum value $V_{MAX}$.

On Fig. 9.2, sketch the variation with angle $\theta$ of the Hall voltage $V_{H}$ for one complete revolution of the probe about axis $XY$.

{{figure:figure_9_2}}

Fig. 9.2
hints: Hint 1: The Hall effect only responds to the component of magnetic flux density perpendicular to the plane of the slice. At $\theta = 0$ this component is maximum - what happens to it as you turn toward 90 degrees?

Hint 2: Think about what happens after 90 degrees when the other face of the slice turns toward the field. How does the direction of charge deflection, and so the sign of $V_H$, change at 180 degrees?
Hint 3: Picture one full turn: maximum positive to zero to maximum negative to zero to maximum positive. What familiar wave shape links those points smoothly?
parts.proper_answer: Sinusoidal (cosine) curve starting at $V_{MAX}$ at $\theta = 0$, zero at $90^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$, $-V_{MAX}$ at $180^{\circ}$, returning to $V_{MAX}$ at $360^{\circ}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the perpendicular component**
Only the component of $B$ normal to the slice deflects the current. If $\theta$ is the rotation from maximum, the effective field is $B \cos\theta$, so $$V_H = V_{MAX} \cos\theta$$ This is why you first rotate to find maximum - field fully perpendicular to slice.

Step 2: **Track key angles**
At $\theta = 0$: full field through slice, $V_H = +V_{MAX}$. At $\theta = 90^{\circ}$: field is in the plane of the slice, no sideways force, $V_H = 0$. At $\theta = 180^{\circ}$: field enters the opposite face, charges deflect the other way, $V_H = -V_{MAX}$. At $\theta = 270^{\circ}$: $V_H = 0$ again. At $\theta = 360^{\circ}$: back to $+V_{MAX}$.

Step 3: **Sketch the shape**
Join these points with a smooth sine wave of one complete cycle. It must cross the $\theta$-axis at $90^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$, have equal positive peak at $0$ and $360^{\circ}$ and equal negative trough at $180^{\circ}$.
